questions.q: What kind of key does the fact table's load join on, for each dimension, to resolve a surrogate key?
options: A random GUID generated at load time
Each dimension's AlternateKey column, which holds the original OLTP source ID
The dimension table's row number
Each dimension's surrogate IDENTITY key directly
questions.explain: The load translates real-world source IDs into warehouse surrogate keys by joining Sales.SalesOrderDetail/Header on each dimension's AlternateKey column (e.g. ProductAlternateKey).

questions.q: Why are dw.FactProductSales's foreign-key constraints added in this lesson instead of when the table was first created?
options: Because Lesson 4 deliberately deferred them until the dimension tables existed and were populated, which only became true after Lesson 5
Because foreign keys must always be added after a table has at least one row
Because SQL Server requires a 24-hour delay before adding constraints
Because Tableau needs the constraints absent to connect
questions.explain: A REFERENCES constraint against a nonexistent table fails. The constraints were deferred since Lesson 4 and are added now that every dimension they reference is built and populated.

questions.q: What does it mean if SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail does not match SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dw.FactProductSales after the load?
options: It's expected and can be ignored
Some order line failed to find a match in one of the load's INNER JOINs and was silently dropped from the warehouse
It means the warehouse has extra rows that don't exist in the source
It means the ALTER TABLE statement failed
questions.explain: A row-count mismatch after an INNER JOIN-based load almost always means a row failed to resolve in one of the joins — most likely an unmatched TerritoryID or CustomerID — and was silently excluded.

questions.q: Why does dw.FactProductSales's load use INNER JOIN while dw.DimProduct's load in Lesson 5 used LEFT JOIN?
options: LEFT JOIN is not supported when loading a fact table
Every order line is expected to have a real product, date, territory, and customer, unlike products which can legitimately have no subcategory
INNER JOIN is simply faster and the choice was made for performance only
There is no real difference between the two in this context
questions.explain: An order line without a resolvable product, date, territory, or customer would represent bad data, not a legitimately missing attribute — so INNER JOIN is the correct, stricter choice here, with the row-count check verifying that expectation held.

questions.q: What is a 'silent join drop,' and why is the row-count parity check the right tool to catch it?
options: A database crash during the load, which always raises a visible error
A feature of LEFT JOIN, not INNER JOIN
A deliberate filter applied to exclude test data
Rows missing from a result because an INNER JOIN found no match, with no error raised — only a direct row-count comparison reveals it
questions.explain: An INNER JOIN that finds no match for a row simply omits it, with no error. Comparing COUNT(*) between source and warehouse is what actually surfaces that gap.
